title: Homogeneity of the Euler characteristic of tensor powers on an abelian variety
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety] of dimension $g\geq1$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], and let $L$ be an invertible $\mathcal O_A$-module [def-sc-invertible-module]. Write $\chi(A,M)=\sum_{i\geq0}(-1)^i\dim_kH^i(A,M)\in\mathbf Z$ for coherent Zariski Euler characteristic [def-pc-euler-characteristic]; for an invertible $M$ this is a finite sum of finite dimensions. For $n\in\mathbf Z$, let $L^{\otimes n}$ mean the usual tensor power for $n>0$, $\mathcal O_A$ for $n=0$, and $(L^{-1})^{\otimes(-n)}$ for $n<0$, where $L^{-1}$ is the tensor inverse of $L$. Then $$\chi(A,L^{\otimes n})=n^g\chi(A,L)\quad\text{for every }n\in\mathbf Z.$$ No ampleness or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed on $L$.

source.place: Chapter I, Theorem 11.1(b), printed p.54 (PDF p.60), tensor-power consequence of abelian Riemann–Roch: for a divisor D representing L, apply the formula to nD for each integer n.

proof.text: By [def-sc-abelian-variety] and [def-weil-proper-morphism], $A$ is proper and finite type over $k$. A field is Noetherian (its only ideals are $0,k$); hence [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] makes $A$ Noetherian. Rank-one local frames [def-sc-invertible-module] show that every signed power $L^{\otimes n}$ is invertible, quasi-coherent and finite type, as is $\mathcal O_A$. By [pqf-lem-coherent-ft-locnoeth] they are coherent. Thus [lem-pc-euler-characteristic-well-defined] gives the finite Euler sums in the statement.

source.place: Tag 01XZ, lemma-coherent-Noetherian; Tag 02O5, proper coherent finiteness; Noetherian permanence is Morphisms Tag 01T6.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-snapper-numerical-polynomial] with $X=A$, $\mathcal F=\mathcal O_A$, $r=1$ and $\mathcal L_1=L$. It gives $P\in\mathbf Q[X]$ with $P(n)=\chi(A,L^{\otimes n})$ for every $n\in\mathbf Z$, including zero and negative exponents. Put $c=\chi(A,L)$; then $P(1)=c$. The numerical polynomial here is on the whole integer lattice, not just the ample or eventual Hilbert function.

source.place: Tag 0BEM, lemma-numerical-polynomial-from-euler (section Tag 0BEL), specialize to one invertible module.

proof.text: Use the representing family of [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus]. For every positive integer $n$, pullback and tensor give $t_x^*(L^{\otimes n})\otimes(L^{\otimes n})^{-1}\cong(t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1})^{\otimes n}$. This identity holds for families over every test scheme, respecting the identity rigidification. Since addition in the represented Picard functor is tensor product, the represented morphisms satisfy $\phi_{L^{\otimes n}}=[n]_{A^\vee}\circ\phi_L$. The cited statement also gives $\dim A^\vee=g$.

source.place: Chapter I §8, dual variety and rigidified invertible-sheaf families, pp.36–40; expand the defining family of the polarization map.

proof.text: For $n>0$, [lem-sc-isogeny-facts] on $A^\vee$ gives $\deg[n]=n^{2g}$. Apply [lem-sfb-isogeny-postcomposition-degree] to $h=\phi_L$ and $u=[n]_{A^\vee}$. With the zero convention even when $\phi_L$ is not an isogeny, step 3 gives $d(\phi_{L^{\otimes n}})=n^{2g}d(\phi_L)$. Apply [lem-sfb-abelian-euler-degree-square] to both invertible sheaves. Consequently $P(n)^2=c^2n^{2g}$ for every positive integer $n$.

source.place: Chapter I Theorem 7.2, p.33; Proposition 7.1, p.32 and degree multiplicativity; Theorem 11.1(a), p.54, with degree-zero convention before Theorem 10.9, p.46.

proof.text: The positive integers are distinct in $\mathbf Q$. By [lem-trf-polynomial-infinite-evaluation-identity], $P^2=c^2X^{2g}$ in $\mathbf Q[X]$. Thus $(P-cX^g)(P+cX^g)=0$. Two nonzero polynomials over $\mathbf Q$ have nonzero product, since the product of their leading coefficients is nonzero; hence $P=cX^g$ or $P=-cX^g$. The second case evaluated at $1$ gives $c=-c$, so $c=0$ and again $P=cX^g$. Evaluate at every integer $n$ and use step 2 and injectivity of $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Q$. This proves the required signed-power identity, including $n=0$ because $g\geq1$.

source.place: Polynomial.eq_of_infinite_eval_eq, lines 156–160; elementary factorization and leading-coefficient argument over Q.
